texts: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game. Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents. Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.

FormalFixer: Intent-Aligned Automated Hardware Repair via Joint Refinement of Specifications, Assertions, and RTL Implementations. Functional errors in hardware designs can compromise correctness and security, and must be fixed before tape-out. Formal property verification (FPV) provides strong guarantees by proving or refuting assertions, but a failed assertion is not always evidence of an RTL defect: the failure may also come from a buggy assertion or from a specification that is semantically correct but too ambiguous or incomplete for direct formalization. This creates a practical repair problem that existing RTL-centric methods do not directly address: the repair loop must align specification intent, verification intent, and RTL behavior before deciding which artifact to change. \textsc{FormalFixer} addresses this problem with a multi-stage, intent-aligned repair workflow for Verilog designs with assertions. It preserves the original specification as authoritative ground truth and appends confidence-filtered refinements to clarify implicit constraints. \textsc{FormalFixer} uses both intent mismatch and verifier-generated counterexample cone graphs to guide iterative RTL patching. This workflow explicitly checks specification--assertion--RTL correspondence. Results support intent alignment for FPV-based hardware repair.

ReliFlow: Reliability-Calibrated Residual Transport for Combinatorial Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction. Predicting the transcriptional response to combined perturbations requires distinguishing interactions between interventions from errors in their individual effect estimates. The latter become more pronounced when single-perturbation evidence is sparse or withheld. We introduce a conditional flow-matching model that estimates the reliability of single-gene effects from training-only cross-fitting and uses those estimates to calibrate the additive source distribution. The velocity is decomposed into a known correction of the additive reference and a learned residual transport field. On Norman genetic perturbations, reduces mean absolute error (MAE) from 0.142 to 0.131 for unseen combinations of observed singles and from 0.198 to 0.178 when constituent singles are withheld. On held-out ComboSciPlex drug combinations, MAE decreases from 0.191 to 0.176. Non-additive residual correlation improves from 0.574 to 0.638, and component ablations identify the contribution of reliability weighting. The results indicate that accounting for uncertain constituent effects improves generalization to unseen genetic and chemical combinations, with a moderate increase in training cost.

Angular Conditional Distillation: Overcoming Classifier Geometry Mismatch. Classifier outputs provide a fundamental and univer- sally available knowledge interface for knowledge distil- lation (KD). However, standard logit objectives entangle transferable semantic relations with architecture-dependent parameterization artifacts, causing a classifier geometry mismatch that makes direct knowledge transfer unreliable. To address this, we propose Angular Conditional Distilla- tion (ACD). First, the Angular Coordinate Interface (ACI) reconstructs the student classifier using angular coordi- nates, suppressing magnitude and bias effects to provide a geometry-compatible space. Then, Scale-Invariant Condi- tional Distillation (SICD) standardizes outputs and exclu- sively transfers conditional non-target relations, filtering out untransferable absolute confidence. Together, ACI de- fines where to transfer, while SICD defines what to transfer. Extensive experiments show that ACD achieves state-of-the- art performance over existing KD methods. Moreover, as a universal drop-in replacement, it consistently improves existing distillation pipelines while requiring no feature adapters or additional inference-time cost. Code is avail- able at https://github.com/laniusnan/ACD.

Can you make models believe false facts in the prompt?. Making LLMs believe false facts is useful for alignment evaluations and for building model organisms. Previous work explored doing so with Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF). But SDF requires fine-tuning one new model for each set of injected false beliefs. To enable larger scale SDF-powered alignment evaluations, we attempt to produce a single model that believes any fact placed in a <facts> tag in the prompt. To do so, we explore doing prompt-conditioned SDF: fine-tuning a model on synthetic documents covering thousands of facts, with each document conditioned on a fact presented in the prompt. We evaluate how deeply the model believes the facts provided in the prompt using evaluations from prior work and a new Jacobian lens evaluation. We find that the belief depth on unseen facts scales roughly log-linearly with the number of training facts, making this a cheap, promising avenue for making models believe false facts, though preliminary experiments on applying it to alignment audits on the small model we studied showed negative results due to these small models often already acting as if they believed facts provided in regular honeypot system prompts. Using RL to reduce the rate at which models verbalize following a false fact in the prompt, on top of prompt-conditioned SDF, generalizes to held-out evals and almost matches SDF on some evaluations. But training against one of our metrics for belief depth makes it harder to trust those evaluations.

Panini- Feasible Grammar For Robot Designs. Symbolic methods make robot designs interpretable but often overlook continuous geometry; learned methods handle geometry but offer less transparent structure. We introduce a typed production grammar that uses case-role relations, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration to generate both manipulation skills and robot morphologies. A geometric realization map translates grammar composition into transformations in SE(3), behaving as a monoid homomorphism when inheritance is inactive and exhibiting a measurable defect when inheritance is enabled. The grammar provides a compact representation, and its arbitration decisions can be recovered from geometric containment (agreement 0.905 +/- 0.062 across 10 seeds, versus 0.611 +/- 0.090 for a Euclidean control). We also introduce PANINI, a cross-entropy search method over grammar-based morphology representations. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PANINI achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. Its main demonstrated advantage is therefore structural rather than optimization performance: grammar-generated designs are legal by construction, and coordinated limb placement produces 95% jointly feasible edits, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for flat parameterization in 6,000 draws. These results show how typed grammars can make robot generation more interpretable and geometrically coordinated, without implying that every feasible design will locomote or that grammar-based search universally outperforms generic optimizers.

FACET - Facet Aware Contrastive Embeddings for Traits- Big Five Estimation from Life Narratives. Personality is only weakly and inconsistently signaled by written language, and existing text-based methods typically combine language-model and psycholinguistic representations at the input or decision level. It remains open whether a more deliberate combination of the two views, and a decomposition of the prediction target, can recover more of the signal. We present a three-phase framework for estimating Big Five personality domain scores from life-narrative interview text. It encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately and combines them by concatenation or by a learned weighting, decomposes each domain into contrastively trained facet embeddings instead of predicting the domain directly, and pools the facet embeddings by attention into a domain-level prediction. We compare end-to-end with staged training and ablate the input modalities, their combination, and the facet-pooling strategy. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (SPAN) study, facet embeddings reach AUC up to 0.740, and domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness. End-to-end training gives lower error than staged training in every domain, and attention pooling gives the lowest error in every domain. Combining the two views lowers error relative to text alone for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness, whereas a learned weighting of the views shows no consistent advantage over concatenation. The framework provides facet- level predictions that a domain-only model cannot, and it improves modestly on a regression from the raw features in four of the five domains.

RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding. While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU. Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.

Structure--Residual Inductive Biases for Language Model Pretraining. Next-token prediction is relied upon to learn both predictive behavior and internal representations. We ask whether representation structure itself should be an explicit inductive bias. Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we study a structure--residual principle in which a representation separates structure from realization detail. We instantiate this principle in two complementary ways. Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) routes information from token segments through boundary carriers while preserving local autoregressive computation. Continuous Concept (CC) regularizes representation geometry and induces a spectral decomposition into low-frequency structure and high-frequency residual. We derive coding bounds for both views and show that multiplicity-corrected boundary attention becomes exact as the within-segment path energy vanishes. Empirically, BBC and CC exhibit strikingly different depth preferences: BBC works best in early layers, whereas CC is most effective in later layers. At 300M training tokens, combining BBC and CC improves NLL by 1.44\% on GPT-2 Medium. These gains persist with training runs up to 20B tokens. Representation diagnostics show that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary states, while CC reduces spectral residual energy. Together, these results suggest that structure--residual biases can improve language-model pretraining beyond next-token prediction. Code: https://github.com/haihuang-ml/structure-residual

Attribution Through the Decoder: Prediction-Space Explanations for Structured Outputs. Networks that predict angles, gaze directions, and rotations do not output these quantities directly: they emit raw coordinates that a fixed decoder, such as normalization, maps to the final prediction. Attribution methods are usually applied to the raw coordinates, so they can credit inputs for changes the decoder discards, such as rescaling a vector when only its direction matters. The resulting explanation can highlight inputs that have no effect on the prediction. We instead attribute through the decoder differential, which for normalization decoders reduces to a scaled tangent projection. We characterize invariance to output rescaling, show that every fixed smooth scalar target on a sphere has points of zero tangential sensitivity, and show that an endpoint-projected variant of Integrated Gradients can still attribute to scale-only inputs, whereas direct angular Integrated Gradients cannot. On synthetic tasks with analytically known relevance, ambient attribution assigns up to 72% of its mass to an irrelevant region. On MPIIGaze validation data, tangent Grad-CAM produces 44% greater prediction displacement under 10% pixel deletion. On PASCAL3D+ with a 6D rotation decoder, the full differential improves mean deletion displacement by 14.1 degrees over the ambient coordinate sum and by 13.8 degrees over a decoder-invariant scalar. Results for a two-polarity tangent LayerCAM variant are mixed: it exceeds ambient-sum LayerCAM on circular regression but no difference is detected on quaternion pose. These results separate two failure sources, radial contamination and scalarization loss. The approach uses existing attribution methods with decoder-aware targets, although some variants also require changes to attribution aggregation. An invariant attribution can still miss inputs that drive the prediction, so invariance and deletion performance should each be checked.

Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting. Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.

What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language. Hierarchical models have been proposed as synthetic settings for studying language. However, their relevance to realistic language corpora remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce tree-grams, autoregressive generative $n$-gram models that build the conditional probability tensor $p(x_n \mid x_{1:n-1})$ through a hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors. $n$ controls the maximal context window, whereas a rank hyperparameter $d$ controls model capacity, yielding an interpretable and systematically scalable family of approximators of language. We show how tree-grams outperform existing $n$-gram baselines, while remaining competitive with deep transformer-based language models. We demonstrate the utility of such controlled approximations by using tree-grams as generative models. In particular, we show that hyperparameter transfer under $μ$P can be made more robust when narrower models are tuned on simpler data, generated by tree-grams with moderate $n$ and $d$. In addition, we show that entropy and effective range of correlations control performance gap after fine-tuning. This is because tree-grams allow us to explicitly control horizon and capacity. When allowed to route across candidate topologies, we observe emergent sparsity in tree-grams. Such concentrated routing permits pruning upto 95\% of topologies without significant change in performance.

Can Activation Steering Substitute for Prompt-Based Affective Priming in LLM Digital Twins?. Affective priming -- asking participants to write about a recalled event, such as a time they felt grateful or lacked control, and then measuring the induced state and its spillover onto related judgments -- is a standard way to manipulate emotion in the social sciences, and it also shifts the responses of LLM-based digital twins. The writing task, however, requires generating a full text. We test whether activation steering can replace it. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 100 personas in two domains (gratitude, lack of control), we compare a real-prompt path replicating the original Twin-2K-500 Mega Study (J2) with an injection path that skips the writing and adds a mean-difference direction, extracted from human writing, to the residual stream at varying strengths. The real-prompt effects fall between the original human and digital-twin effects in 5 of 6 comparisons. Injection shifts the manipulation check in a dose-dependent way and matches the real-prompt effect at one strength in the gratitude domain (beta ~ 2.7), but overshoots beyond it, on the proximal measure as well, and asymmetrically across the two directions. A structure-matched No-Injection baseline separates two sources of difference: omitting the writing task raises the proximal measure in both domains, whereas the injected direction itself moves a distal measure in the lack-of-control domain. Substitution is therefore measure-dependent: validity established for one way of inducing a state does not carry over uniformly to another.

Cross-cultural Adaptation of Recipes for Low-Resource Languages: A Benchmark and Multilingual Culinary Lexicon for Hausa, Yorùbá, and Igbo. Recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) have improved machine translation, yet culturally adaptive translation for low-resource languages (LRLs) remains underexplored. This is particularly challenging for recipes, where ingredients, cooking tools, measurements, and procedures may require adaptation to the target cultural context. In this work, we introduce ReciLoReL, a benchmark of 600 expert-translated and culturally adapted recipes across Yorùbá, Hausa, and Igbo (three of the most prominent languages in Nigeria), and ReciLex, a multilingual culinary lexicon containing approximately 15,000 translated entities across ten recipe entity categories, including ingredients, tools, chef actions, state of tools, and durations. We evaluate state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs for English-to-LRL recipe translation under zero-shot and few-shot settings and investigate whether augmenting LLMs with ReciLex improves culturally adaptive recipe translation without requiring large target-language recipe corpora for training or fine-tuning. Beyond conventional reference-based translation evaluation using BLEU, chrF, and TER, we introduce five criteria for evaluating cultural adaptation, adapted from established cross-cultural adaptation methods. Across the selected LLMs and languages, ReciLex improves average BLEU from 13.57 to 14.51 and chrF from 37.89 to 38.74, while reducing TER from 77.14 to 75.12. Human evaluation further shows improvements ranging from 0.11 to 0.36 points across the five cultural adaptation evaluation criteria on a five-point scale. Overall, our work provides new resources, evaluation criteria, and empirical evaluation for studying culturally adaptive recipe translation in low-resource settings.

Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization. Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand- engineered. We present Meta-RTL, an EDA-grounded framework that evolves RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop while keeping the optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL* reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70% of them. Without further evolution, Meta-RTL* transfers to 10 unseen IC-RTL designs, reducing aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and total synthesized area by 12.6%. We further characterize three search mechanisms in the evolved harness and assess their contributions through ablations and a case study.

GRODE-RTL: Source-Mapped Dependency Views for LLM-Based RTL Repair. Large Language Models show great potential for automated Register-Transfer Level repair, yet they struggle with non-local faults where root causes and failing outputs reside far apart in source code. Treating RTL as a flat token sequence obscures hardware dataflows, whereas exposing complete synthesized graphs overwhelms the model with fine-grained metadata. To resolve this representation dilemma, we propose GRODE-RTL, an anchor-centric representation that extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps netlist nodes back to editable source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view. By prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant hops, GRODE-RTL guides standard tool-using agents without exposing ground-truth hints or oracle feedback. We evaluate GRODE-RTL across 30 formally validated non-local faults using three LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3) alongside a controlled six-configuration ablation study. GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek, by 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and by 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on the hard-to-retrieve far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets of all three models. Our controls isolate structural relevance from generic context expansion, proving that selective dependency organization rather than full graph exposure is key to effective RTL repair.

ReLay: Bidirectional Layout-Code Translation and Library Evolution for Reusable and Process-Portable Analog Design. Analog layout generators provide a programmable interface for design reuse and process migration, but their coverage is limited by handcrafted libraries. The designer knowledge embedded in complete layouts remains implicit in their geometry, making it difficult to capture in reusable generator libraries. We present ReLay, a bidirectional layout-code framework that recovers generator programs from existing layouts, enabling cross-PDK portability and parametric resizing of existing designs. Constructions that recur across recovered programs are promoted to library functions, so the library evolves as layouts accumulate. We also introduce the first layout-code benchmark: 1,050 hand-drawn layouts from 27 circuit families across three open-source PDKs, ranging from primitive cells to full chips. Learned functions account for 53-66% of layout-building calls in held-out layouts, demonstrating reuse beyond the learning corpus. Frontier LLM agents use ReLay to produce new layouts at 64-77% lower API cost per completed task than direct geometry generation, with comparable completion rates and electrical quality.

Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.

One UWB Radar, Many Views: Comparing and Fusing Signal Representations for Human Activity Recognition. IEEE 802.15.4z-compliant impulse-radio ultra-wideband (IR-UWB) transceivers are increasingly built into consumer devices, enabling contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR) in healthcare. Before activity classification, the signal is typically converted into range-time, range-Doppler, or time-Doppler maps, each exposing different spatial and motion cues. Existing comparisons often apply shared processing across representations, leaving it unclear whether their rankings hold after independent tuning. It is also unknown whether rankings and fusion gains generalize across environments and activities, and at what computational cost. Consequently, practitioners lack guidance on which representation and processing suit a given HAR deployment. We release an open dataset of raw IR-UWB measurements collected by a ceiling-mounted radar from 44 participants during scripted activity sequences in 12 layouts across two bedrooms. Using a statistically guided, staged search, we independently tune each representation across five processing and deployment settings. We then compare individual and fused performance under layout and room shifts and quantify computational cost. Across over 1{,}000 cross-validated models, independent tuning proves essential, as optimal processing differs per representation and processing choices shift macro-F1 by up to 26 points, four times the gap between representations. Once tuned, the range-Doppler map leads for unseen layouts (85.1\% macro-F1), while time-Doppler map does for unseen rooms (72.7\%). Fusing all three maps raises these scores to 89.1\% and 80.0\%, respectively. Lower sampling rates and narrower Doppler bands reduce latency by 38--51\% with at most a 1.5-point macro-F1 loss. The best representation for UWB HAR is therefore a deployment decision, not a fixed property.

texts: LAaDT-DSS: decision support for non-experts on rooftop PV, incentive and grid simulations under Turkish tariff rules. Rooftop photovoltaics raise three questions: should a household invest, which incentive costs the state least, and does the feeder stay within limits? Those who ask are rarely modellers. We present LAaDT-DSS, decision-support software that answers all three under Turkish tariff rules from one simulation core. Non-experts reach it by clicking a house on a 3D map or by asking in plain words; a language model is asked to call the simulation tools, not to compute. Each entry of its 125-entry parameter registry is marked as sourced or estimated. Case studies test the system. Its PV yield lies within $\pm$3.6% of two independent tools at equal losses. Across 2,048 draws of its estimated inputs, the answer for PV alone held in all but one; with a battery, it changed in 31-41% of the draws. Four scripted chat scenarios ran end to end; no user study was run.

When Figures Disagree with Text: Evaluating Autonomous Visual Evidence Verification in Scientific Papers. Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure shows. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.

Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection. Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

MEM-STRESS: Longitudinal Field Study of a Wearable-Informed AI Chatbot for Stress Management. Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control). Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.

Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks. Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the layout of each figure, locating the diffraction plot and its curves and sketching a coarse trace of each, while classical computer vision (CV) refines every trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 COF articles, the pipeline produces 11,445 calibrated diffraction curves, released in the open database COF-PEAK. Compared with a hand digitization of 60 panels, extracted peak positions differ by a median of only 0.07 degrees. Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.

AllotNet: an Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Choice Model for Moral Judgement in Humanitarian Aid Allocation, Validated against a Planted Synthetic Population. Official development assistance fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025, and the decision of who is helped first when there is not enough for everyone is moving into software. A leading published machine-learning targeting system excluded 53 per cent of eligible households as deployed. If the rule of distribution ends up in code, it should carry the judgement of many cultures, and the machine should execute while a person judges. AllotNet is an interpretable mixture-of-experts conditional logit for the allocation judgements elicited by Allot, a pre-registered six-language instrument: eight linear taste experts over seven ethical criteria, weighted by a gate over participant context, with a damped residual, an encoder for household intake, an outcome head and a budget-constrained planner that builds a review queue and never rejects anyone. A model of human judgement has no answer key on real data, so we wrote one first: a planted synthetic population of 5.6 million sessions and 104 million responses (98 million usable choices), generated by the production code path from a ground truth hidden from the loss. All sixteen pre-specified checks passed: criterion ranking $ρ= 1.000$, hidden segments recovered (ARI 0.671), outcome head at 99 per cent of the noise ceiling, planner at 99.4 per cent of oracle. The caveats are reported with them: two checks are weaker than their titles, and a live-generation failure cost 260,712 seeds. The model has 23,550 parameters, is trained quantisation-aware for NVFP4 with its interpretable core in fp32 (welfare-rank parity $ρ= 0.9937$ at W4A16 on the shipped bundle; one parity threshold was relaxed post hoc), and ships as a 125 KB bundle with C11, Java, Rust and Python runtimes. Nothing has been trained on real data yet; at the study's real scale a hierarchical Bayesian mixed logit is the registered comparator.

Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization. Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.

Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

Stress Testing a Multimodal Large Language Model Grading Assistant on Kinematics Graph Reading. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recognize graph features yet award credit without sufficient graphical support. This exploratory study examines selected grading outputs for synthetic responses to four kinematics exercises, generated through visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs. Different model and prompt configurations were used. Some judgments correctly distinguished instantaneous zero velocity from rest over a finite interval and recognized positive curvature. Yet a severely distorted velocity--time graph received full credit despite disconnected and branching traces and an unclear zero-velocity reference. Other submissions graded under the same configuration lost substantial credit. Numerical cutoffs intended to distinguish meaningful features from drawing irregularities were supplied without a coordinate convention for unnumbered graphs, leaving the basis of exact partial-credit awards unresolved. Stress testing can expose unsupported awards before classroom use. For the configurations examined, we do not recommend accepting scores as final grades without instructor review, including review of full-credit responses.

Deep Discriminative Feature Fusion of Convolutional and Attention-Based Recurrent Representations for Subject-Independent ECG Stress Recognition. Stress has become a significant concern because of its negative impact on both physical and mental health and therefore drives the need for reliable automated systems to assess stress levels. Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals provide a non-invasive and objective measure of physiological stress responses and have emerged as a promising modality for continuous stress monitoring. While deep learning techniques have achieved encouraging results in ECG-based stress detection, many studies focus only on one type of feature representation, and therefore limit their ability to capture both the morphological patterns and temporal dynamics embedded in ECG signals. To address this limitation, in this paper, we propose three deep learning-based feature fusion frameworks for ECG-based stress classification. These are Residual Feature Fusion (RFF), Bidirectional Feature-Wise Cross-Attention Fusion (BFCAF), and a novel Cross-Attention Residual Fusion (CARF) framework that combines the strengths of residual learning and bidirectional cross-attention within a unified architecture. A 1D Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN) and a BiLSTM-Attention network are used to extract complementary morphological and temporal representations from ECG signals, respectively. The proposed fusion frameworks leverage these heterogeneous representations to improve feature interaction, information preservation, and stress discrimination. The proposed frameworks are evaluated using subject-independent Leave-One-Subject-Out Cross-Validation (LOSOCV) on the RML and WESAD datasets for three-class stress classification. Experimental results show that the proposed feature fusion methods consistently improve performance over individual CNN and BiLSTM models, with CARF achieving the highest accuracies of 83.1% and 77.91% on the RML and WESAD datasets, respectively.

SciFig2Data: A Workflow for Recovering Structured Data from Scientific Figures. Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.

texts: CounselTraj: Synthesizing Process-Aware Psychological Counseling Dialogues via Dialogue-Act Trajectory Planning. The growing demand for psychological counseling has motivated the development of LLM-based systems that support human counselors, but training such systems requires large-scale, high-quality dialogue data. Authentic counseling transcripts are difficult to collect and share because of privacy concerns, making synthetic dialogues an important alternative. However, existing synthetic datasets, despite covering diverse scenarios and client profiles, often consist of brief exchanges and fail to capture session-level counseling processes. We propose CounselTraj, a dialogue-act trajectory planning framework for expanding brief synthetic dialogues into process-aware, session-level psychological counseling dialogues. CounselTraj learns dialogue-act patterns from role-play counseling dialogues produced by human counselors, plans coordinated trajectories for clients and counselors, and uses them as flexible guidance for long-form dialogue generation. Experiments across three Chinese synthetic counseling datasets show that CounselTraj produces more complete and coherent sessions with higher-quality counselor interventions than both direct expansion and expansion with randomly sampled trajectories. Based on CounselTraj, we construct CounselTrajD, a dataset containing over 10K process-guided Chinese psychological counseling dialogues, and use it to train CounselTrajLM for counseling response generation. Evaluations at both the response and session levels show that CounselTrajLM outperforms publicly available Chinese counseling models in response quality, therapeutic understanding and intervention, and counseling-process coherence and progress. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/UEC-InabaLab/CounselTraj.

PeriaTrace: Tooth-Level Grounding Diagnosis and Patient-Facing Explanations from Periapical Radiographs. Periapical radiographs (PRs) are central to endodontic diagnosis, but interpreting them and preparing reports are time-consuming. Technical language can limit patients' understanding, while existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. We present PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework integrating tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations and care recommendations. PeriaTrace was developed and evaluated using 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. In internal evaluation, it achieved a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35%, BLEU-4 of 0.6504, an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and a grounding-tag F1 score of 77.93%. In the two external cohorts, senior endodontists considered 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per PR, several tens of times faster than manual drafting. Among 196 survey participants without medical backgrounds, 96.4% preferred reports with plain-language explanations and care recommendations, and 84.7% found visual localization cues helpful. PeriaTrace may enable faster, evidence-traceable reporting while supporting clinical review and patient communication. (Abridged version)

OICycle: Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle for Belief-State Learning in Longitudinal Clinical Decision Making. Clinical care is a closed loop: clinicians observe partial evidence, infer the patient's state, and intervene, and each intervention determines what is observed next. This makes clinical decision making a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which a belief over a latent patient state must be updated from irregular, multimodal, and incomplete records. Yet most deep clinical models predict from a single snapshot or from coarsely aggregated history, while POMDP-based clinical methods need hand-specified discrete state spaces and transition models that real electronic health records cannot supply. We introduce OICycle (Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle), which learns a stochastic belief state directly from retrospective trajectories. At every episode, a learned recurrent operator fuses a sample of the previous belief with the new multimodal observations and the intervention that produced them. The resulting Gaussian belief is trained to predict clinicians' next interventions, the time to the next episode, and next-episode mortality. To enable reproducible evaluation, we release a benchmark derived from MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-Note, and MIMIC-CXR that organizes 72,075 hospital admissions (5.4M laboratory, microbiology, radiology, prescription, and note records) into temporally ordered therapeutic--diagnostic episodes. Compared with an otherwise identical history-free model, OICycle improves next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347, time-to-next-episode macro-F1 from 0.293 to 0.351, and next-episode mortality macro-F1 from 0.585 to 0.649. Analysis shows that the learned belief encodes intervention type and trajectory position and evolves smoothly across episodes, and that the benefit of history is concentrated in interventions whose ordering depends on prior findings.

On the Creation of Object-Centric Event Logs from Patient Journeys. Interactions between patients and health systems as well as conditions that individuals experience during a disease are represented in patient journeys. Therefore, patient journeys are important assets to investigate how care is being provided, and how health systems can be designed to better suit the needs of patients. While there is initial work on patient journeys from a process mining perspective with traditional case notions, object-centric process mining techniques have yet to be covered. This is unfortunate, since due to the rich structure of objects and their relationships, object-centric process mining approaches are particularly promising in this context. This paper addresses this gap by investigating object-centric event log (OCEL) generation from patient journeys. Based on a list of challenges and requirements, the paper presents an approach for the creation of OCELs from patient journey data. The approach is evaluated on a synthetic patient cohort provided by our industry partner.

Right Destination, Wrong Journey: Synthetic Counseling Dialogues Miss Human Interactional Dynamics. LLM-generated counseling dialogues are increasingly used for training and evaluating mental-health systems, yet existing evaluations focus largely on response quality and final outcomes rather than how support unfolds over time. We conduct a trajectory-centered evaluation of process fidelity across ten human, reconstructed, and synthetic counseling datasets. Our results show that synthetic dialogues often reach plausible endpoints but differ from human support in recovery dynamics and turn-by-turn responsiveness. While generation design can shift global properties such as recovery timing and trajectory structure, contingent patient--counselor responsiveness remains consistently lower in fidelity across models and generation paradigms. Our experiments on controlled synthetic datasets show that targeted generation interventions can narrow the gap with real data on several trajectory-level measures, but do not fully recover interactional fidelity, with turn-level responsiveness remaining limited. We release three controlled synthetic datasets comprising 2,050 dialogues, together with annotations and the evaluation framework.

texts: SpiderMark: Hybrid Watermarking for Generative AI via Algorithmic Injection and Learning-Based Verification. The proliferation of diffusion-based generative models has intensified the need for reliable methods to trace and verify the provenance of AI-generated images. Existing watermarking approaches for diffusion models typically rely on isotropic frequency patterns and handcrafted detection metrics, which are prone to directional vulnerability and threshold instability across diverse image transformations. We propose SpiderMark, a hybrid watermarking framework that combines algorithmic frequency-domain injection with learning-based probabilistic verification, requiring no modifications to pretrained diffusion model weights. SpiderMark embeds a structured spider-web pattern, comprising radial spokes and concentric polygonal rings, into the Fourier representation of the initial latent noise, and trains a lightweight ResNet-18 verifier augmented with auxiliary similarity cues (PSNR and L1) to produce a continuous watermark confidence score for watermark detection. Across nine evaluation conditions, SpiderMark achieves the highest fixed-threshold Accuracy in eight, while retaining strong detection on unseen COCO prompts without verifier retraining. CLIP similarity and FID measurements show that these detection gains are accompanied by small measured differences in prompt alignment and distributional image quality. SpiderMark establishes that structured watermark geometry and learned probabilistic verification can be unified into a single, practical framework, bridging the gap between imperceptibility, robustness, and real-world verifiability for generative AI content attribution.

LAGR: Language-Aware Grasp Re-Ranking for Task Oriented Grasping. Grasping is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with the appropriate grasp depending on the downstream task. For example, a hammer should be held by its handle for hammering but by its head when it is handed over. Selecting such a grasp requires consideration of two criteria: physical feasibility on the object and suitability for the task. Developing such an approach requires dense grasp labels with both feasibility and task scores on real observations, but existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate. To address this gap, we construct a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs from $17$ object categories. Additionally, we introduce LAGR, a task-oriented grasp detection method that explicitly addresses both these challenges. Given vision-language inputs, LAGR first generates task-independent grasp proposals along with a physical feasibility score, and then scores the generated grasps with a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly. Experiments show that LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points. We further validate LAGR on real objects by executing task-oriented grasps with a Franka Research 3 robot.

TOGBench: Benchmarking and Improving Tiny-Object Generation Fidelity in Aerial Imagery. Advances in deep generative models now enable the synthesis of realistic imagery. However, aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects, such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft, which occupy only a few pixels owing to the overhead, wide-area nature of aerial imaging. Existing generative models struggle substantially more with tiny objects than with larger ones. This limitation has been overlooked, as prior work on generative evaluation emphasizes prompt following or human preference rather than whether small objects are rendered faithfully. To address this gap, we introduce TOGBench, a quantitative, object-level benchmark for evaluating tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial imagery. We further propose two simple train-/inference-time techniques that improve the ability of layout-to-image generators to render small objects, raising their performance on TOGBench.

Say Less, Hallucinate Less? Diagnosing and Restoring Object Coverage in Preference-Optimized Vision-Language Models. Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models. We find that four public PO checkpoints of LLaVA-1.5-7B also lower object coverage. They name fewer object categories, and their lower hallucination rates bring no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR. We therefore ask how much of the PO gain the base model can reproduce by stopping earlier. A positive end-of-sequence (EOS) logit bias lets the base model reach the recall of each PO model, and this early stopping alone reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three checkpoints on two disjoint COCO sets. Writing longer does not bring the lost categories back. Under greedy decoding, a negative EOS bias recovers only 2 to 9 percent of the lost CHAIR recall of these checkpoints, and 94 to 96 percent of the added object mentions repeat categories already named. On CHAIR, the base caption of the same image still names about half of the missed object categories. We therefore propose base-guided object-category restoration, which appends high-confidence base-only categories to the PO caption without training. With thresholds fixed on a development set, it brings three checkpoints within one point of the base recall on a held-out COCO set with a lower distinct-object hallucination rate than the base model. Against the recall-matched base stopping curve, its gain holds for RLAIF-V near the base recall and for RLAIF-V and CHAIR-DPO at an intermediate recall. We will release the code of the recall-controlled evaluation.

Image Watermarking With Memory Across Reissuance. Publishers often revise and reissue images, yet valid watermarks may persist on superseded releases or unapproved edits. Even a current release can contain regions last authorized at different revisions. We introduce and formalize reissuable provenance: determining an image's current, superseded, or unissued status and recovering each region's last authorized revision (its generation), with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Generational Stratigraphy Fields (GSF) combine watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, enabling replacement or retirement without rewriting circulated copies. Each reissue freshly embeds new generation labels in approved regions and inherited labels elsewhere, preserving history without requiring old watermarks to survive successive edits. Our complete-output reissuance evaluation follows 480 histories through four releases, retaining each AI editor's entire output. GSF achieves 99.67% accuracy in classifying issued images as current or superseded and 94.09% recall of unissued edits. After three reissues, one generation map provides time and location: it recovers regional labels with 93.13% median accuracy and localizes the latest approved revision with 92.86% IoU. Regional labels remain readable under tested delivery transformations that impair issued-state recognition. Watermarks can thus express who issued an image, which release is authoritative now, and when each region was last authorized.

A tiny object detection dataset for high-altitude open-water search and rescue. Large aerial platforms often operate above 1.5 km to improve the efficiency of open water search and rescue (OW-SAR). However, long imaging distances, wide fields of view, and limited sensor resolution reduce objects to a few pixels, increasing their susceptibility to environmental interference and making detection harder than for conventional small objects. To our knowledge, existing datasets focus on low-altitude scenarios and do not support automatic detection at 1.5-2.0 km. We therefore present TinyWOD, a tiny object detection dataset for high-altitude OW-SAR using lifebuoys as detection targets. It comprises 11,359 manually annotated images and 19,505 annotated instances spanning diverse environments, lighting conditions, water colors, and surface ripples. Compared with existing datasets, TinyWOD contains much smaller objects and a substantially higher proportion of tiny instances; its average equivalent side length (ESL) is 12.7 pixels, with 76.96% of in stances having ESLs below 15 pixels, reflecting actual high-altitude water-rescue imaging conditions. We define APtiny, a tiny object detection metric, and benchmark mainstream and state-of-the-art networks using this and conventional metrics. All evaluated networks effectively detect tiny waterborne objects, demonstrating TinyWOD's reusability and utility. We expect this dataset to support research on tiny object detection in high-altitude OW-SAR.

Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models. Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.

Mind the Gaps: State-Guided Supervision Allocation for Object Detection Dataset Distillation. Recent advances in dataset distillation have enabled large-scale training datasets to be compressed into compact synthetic sets. However, dataset distillation for object detection remains challenging, as it requires preserving diverse classification and localization signals under limited image budgets. Existing approaches often emphasize individual-image informativeness without explicitly accounting for supervision accumulated across the distilled dataset, potentially leading to redundant supervision and uneven class-scale coverage. To address this limitation, we propose State-Guided Supervision Allocation (SGSA), a framework that formulates object detection dataset distillation as a dataset-level progressive supervision allocation problem. SGSA establishes class-scale supervision quotas and maintains a global state that tracks detector predictions accumulated from previously selected synthetic images. The remaining gaps between the target quotas and accumulated supervision guide adaptive object sampling, detector-guided canvas refinement, and marginal-gain-based candidate selection, encouraging complementary supervision across images. On MS COCO, SGSA outperforms a matched OD3 baseline by 3.73-4.06 mAP points across three image budgets (0.25%-1.0%). On PASCAL VOC, SGSA outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by 4.53-6.90 mAP50 points across three image budgets. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of dataset-level supervision allocation guided by accumulated detector feedback under limited image budgets.

LexiDet-OVD: Benchmarking Lexical Sensitivity in Open-Vocabulary Object Detection. Open-vocabulary object detectors localize objects from free-form text prompts, but their reliability depends on how users describe the target. Standard evaluations usually test a fixed class name, leaving prompt-induced failure modes underexplored. We introduce LexiDet-OVD, a benchmark and metric suite for studying lexical sensitivity in open-vocabulary object detection. We organize prompt sets into equivalent, conditional, and broad semantic scopes, and evaluate four detector families on fixed COCO and LVIS samples, each covering 30 classes (800 held-out COCO images and 1,000 LVIS images). Beyond mean and worst-prompt AP50, we report P10, CVaR at 20%, leave-one-prompt-out influence, detection agreement, box consistency, and confidence variance using one-to-one multi-instance matching. Equivalent-prompt best-to-worst gaps range from 5.3 to 23.4 points on COCO1000 and from 5.1 to 29.9 points on LVIS1000-30c, showing that strong average accuracy and lexical stability are distinct properties. We compare maximum-score selection, weighted-box fusion, Prompt Consensus, and an exploratory fusion rule. Aggregation recovers performance in several settings, but no method dominates all model-dataset pairs. A controlled Detic/SHiNe comparison further shows that semantic hierarchy enrichment does not by itself eliminate lexical sensitivity. These results support reporting prompt-distribution robustness alongside conventional open-vocabulary detection accuracy.

RSWP: Robust SO(3)-Equivariant Watermarking for Panoramic Images. Robust watermarking for panoramic imagery is impeded by the topological mismatch between spherical signals and planar representations. Conventional methods fail under $SO(3)$ viewing rotations due to non-linear geometric warping and struggle with viewport extraction, which typically necessitates computationally expensive inverse remapping. To address these challenges, we propose RSWP, a watermarking framework grounded in icosahedral group theory. Leveraging the property that the icosahedral group ($\mathcal{I}_{60}$) serves as the largest discrete subgroup of $SO(3)$, we decompose spherical rotations into tractable local planar rotations and combinatorial facet permutations. Accordingly, we introduce a decoupling architecture that embeds watermarks into discrete facets and a theoretically guaranteed Equivariance-to-Invariance decoding paradigm. By employing an equivariant feature extractor followed by a permutation-invariant sorting module, this paradigm rigorously synchronizes rotation-distorted features. Moreover, the dual-extractor design inherently supports direct, blind watermark retrieval from partial 2D renderings without geometric calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSWP achieves state-of-the-art robustness against continuous $SO(3)$ rotations and viewport transformations while preserving high visual fidelity.

Beyond Rigid Hands: Deforming Skin into Contact-Consistent Hand Meshes. Hands grasp objects with soft skin. A fingertip flattens against a mug, and a palm curves around a bottle. Yet hand-object datasets and estimators represent the hand as a rigid articulated mesh, which hovers above or penetrates the object where skin would press against it. Existing refiners keep the mesh rigid and adjust only the pose, trading pose accuracy for physical plausibility. We ask whether a rigid hand can instead touch the object as skin does while staying close to its original pose. We lift annotated or estimated rigid hands to contact-consistent meshes through an optimization that (i) slightly adjusts the joints and wrist to bring the fingers onto the object, (ii) deforms the skin so that penetrating regions settle onto the surface, and (iii) keeps this deformation consistent over time. Since deformation reaches only skin already near the object, we further train a lightweight head on the lifted annotations to predict where an estimated hand should touch and steer the deformation there. Unlike existing refiners, the lift more than doubles the skin lying on the object surface for three published estimators while barely changing the pose. Guidance from the learned head further improves grasp stability by closing contact gaps that the estimate leaves open. Existing hand-object datasets and estimators can thus adopt contact-consistent hands without changing the hand model or retraining the estimators.
